title: The scroll
hook: a monkey that lets go of every branch, and still can't stop
tomorrow: a house full of noise: can real quiet live there at all?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a city with six open gates and mindfulness posted at each one. Guard the door. Today, the thumb that keeps going.

A feed has no bottom. One more video, one more post, and the thumb moves before anyone decides. An old verse saw this, long before glass screens. It's in the Dhammapada, in the chapter on thirst: "The thirst of a thoughtless man grows like a creeper; he runs from life to life, like a monkey seeking fruit in the forest." Read it twice and something is odd. A monkey lets go of every branch it grabs. Letting go is the whole way it travels. So if it already lets go all day long, what exactly is the trouble?
screen: `A FEED WITH NO BOTTOM.` → `A MONKEY IN THE FOREST.` → `IT ALREADY LETS GO. SO WHAT'S WRONG?`

segments.voice: Another sutta draws the same monkey more closely. It roams the forest, grabs a branch, lets it go, and grabs another. That, the Buddha says, is how the restless mind moves: one thing, then the next, day and night. So here's the answer to the puzzle. The monkey lets go only to grab. Its hand is never empty for a moment. Each release is already the reach for the next branch. A scroll works just like that. Closing one video is the swipe to the next. The thumb isn't holding anything long, and it's never put down. Now look back at the verse. The trouble isn't fruit; forests are full of fruit, and some of it is good. The trouble is the word thoughtless. The creeper grows quietly while nobody's watching, and the monkey keeps leaping because nobody stops to ask if it's hungry. The verse keeps both pictures because craving moves both ways: slow like the vine, fast like the leap. Craving, tanha, the thirst, is the name for that pull to the next and the next. So putting it down is different from letting go. Letting go, the monkey does all day. Putting it down means the hand stays open, and empty, for one moment longer than it wants to. In that gap, the question can finally arrive: was I hungry for this at all?
screen: `GRAB, LET GO, GRAB AGAIN.` · `THE HAND IS NEVER EMPTY.` · `THE TROUBLE IS THOUGHTLESS.` · `AN OPEN HAND, ONE MOMENT LONGER.` · then, large: `PUT IT DOWN.`

segments.voice: Set down whatever is in your hands and rest them on your knees, palms up and open. When they want to reach for something, the phone, a sleeve, your hair, leave them open for one more breath. Let empty hands be the whole practice for the sit.
The scroll: the monkey's way, letting go of one branch only to grab the next, with a hand that's never empty.
The line to keep: put it down, and leave the hand empty a little longer. Five of nine in the mind at home.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the monkey as a picture of the restless mind; practitioners work with it by noticing the urge to reach and pausing before acting on it.

notes: Puzzle shape: the odd detail is that the monkey already lets go of every branch; the answer (it lets go only to grab) draws on SN 12.61. Confirm the bridge between Dhp 334 and SN 12.61 reads fairly.

'The forest is full of fruit, and some of it is good' is a gentle reading, not a claim of the verse; confirm it doesn't soften the teaching on craving too far.
